Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of natural disaster. A car-crash-specific trigger suggests a different index trauma unless there is clear disaster-related context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear, vulnerability, dissociation/gaps, and interpersonal mistrust after a natural disaster. Intense rage could occur clinically, but here it lacks corroboration from threat or appraisal items and weakens overall coherence.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'related people' as a primary trigger is hard to justify unless they were directly linked to the event; with no supporting interpersonal trauma content elsewhere, this trigger is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The threat item about unusual silence implying imminent danger fits combat/interpersonal danger contexts more than natural disaster exposure, and it is not supported by the trigger or appraisal content here.

vignette:
Liam Fischer is a 29-year-old salesman who came to treatment months after surviving a natural disaster during a weekend hiking trip with friends. Before it happened, he had thought of himself as easygoing, sociable, and good at handling whatever came up. He was the kind of person who could talk comfortably to strangers all day for work and still have energy left for friends afterward. The disaster occurred in a wooded mountain area that had felt, until then, like the opposite of danger. What he remembers clearly is how quickly the setting changed: open air, trees, wet ground, the sense that nature had become something unpredictable and overpowering. In the middle of that chaos, he experienced intense fear that he was not safe and that the people around him might not be able to help him. When he tries to speak about that day now, his account becomes uneven. There are stretches he can describe with striking emotional force and then blank sections he cannot fill in, no matter how hard he tries. He says there are parts that are simply missing.

In the weeks afterward, Liam was unsettled by how the experience returned. Sometimes it was not a picture or a full memory at all, but the same wave of terror in his body, arriving all at once as if the disaster were happening again. At other times, when he did try to remember, what came back was not distant recollection but the original fear itself, so immediate that he would stop talking mid-sentence and look around the room. He found this especially disturbing because he could not always connect the feeling to a clear image. He would suddenly feel the full force of panic, dread, and helplessness without being able to say exactly what moment he was reliving. That lack of coherence frightened him as much as the memory itself. He began to think that something fundamental in him had changed, that he no longer knew who he was if he could be taken over so completely by fear and not even understand it.

His work as a salesperson made it hard to avoid the world. He spent much of the day driving to different parts of town, walking into office parks, retail spaces, and unfamiliar buildings, keeping up a personable, confident front. Physical locations began to matter in ways they never had before. Certain places, especially open outdoor commercial sites, roadside stretches near tree lines, and properties on the edge of undeveloped land, made him tense before he had consciously registered why. On days when a client meeting required him to visit a more rural account or a landscaped development with heavy greenery, he would feel himself go on guard as soon as he pulled into the lot. He scanned exits, checked the terrain, noticed weather, and remained alert to where he could move if something happened. He could usually get through the meeting, but colleagues had started to comment that he seemed distracted or unusually serious.

Outside work, he changed his life more dramatically. He stopped joining friends for camping trips, hikes, or even casual park gatherings. Being in nature no longer felt restorative; it felt too similar to where it happened. Even walking through a wooded trail in a local park could make him feel exposed. He also avoided situations in which he felt emotionally open or dependent. Dating fell away, and even with close friends he kept conversations on the surface. Feeling vulnerable in any sense had become a trigger in itself. If he felt too emotionally exposed-if someone asked how he had really been, or if he noticed himself needing comfort-he became keyed up and withdrawn. He had come to believe that relying on other people was dangerous or pointless. In his mind, when things truly went wrong, other people could not be counted on.

Sleep became another place where he no longer felt secure. He woke abruptly during the night and checked the apartment to make sure he was safe, sometimes more than once. He looked at the windows, the locks, the hallway outside his bedroom. He knew on one level that he was in his own home, but his body behaved as if danger might still break in without warning. During the day he remained superalert, scanning his surroundings in restaurants, parking lots, and client offices. This constant watchfulness left him exhausted and detached. What troubled him most was not only the fear, but the hollowing out that had followed it. He said that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. Work felt like performance, friendships felt distant, and the future looked flat.

Liam finally sought help after a work trip to meet a client at a property on the outskirts of town bordered by woods. Standing in that setting, he was suddenly overtaken by the sense that the disaster was happening again. For a few moments he was no longer just anxious; he was back inside the original terror. He managed to leave and sit in his car until it passed, but afterward he was shaken by how little control he had felt. He came to treatment afraid that this version of himself-guarded, distrustful, emptied out, and perpetually braced-might be permanent. At the same time, he said he was hoping, cautiously, to understand why his mind still reacted as if he were there and whether it was possible to feel like himself again.
